# Sex Differences in the Association Between Lipoprotein(a) and Cardiovascular Outcomes: The MGB Lp(a) Registry

**Authors:** Gurleen Kaur; Adam N Berman; David W Biery; Stephanie A Besser; Wanda Y Wu; Brittany Weber; Michael C Honigberg; Khurram Nasir; Martha Gulati; Marcelo F Di Carli; Leslee J Shaw; Deepak L Bhatt; Ron Blankstein

**Affiliations:** 1 Department of Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA | 2 Division of Cardiovascular Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA | 3 Albert Einstein College of Medicine, New York, NY | 4 Department of Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA | 5 Division of Cardiology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA | 6 Division of Cardiovascular Prevention and Wellness, Department of Cardiovascular Medicine, Houston Methodist DeBakey Heart and Vascular Center, Houston, TX | 7 Barbra Streisand Women’s Heart Center, Smidt Heart Institute, Department of Cardiology, Cedars‐Sinai Smidt Heart Institute, Los Angeles, CA | 8 Blavatnik Family Women’s Research Institute, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY | 9 Mount Sinai Fuster Heart Hospital, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY

## Abstract

Sex‐based differences in the association of lipoprotein(a) with cardiovascular outcomes have not been well established for those without prior atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

Patients with no baseline atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease were identified in the MGB (Mass General Brigham) Lp(a) Registry, a retrospective cohort of patients who had lipoprotein(a) measured from 2000 to 2019. Lipoprotein(a) percentile groups were categorized as 1st to 50th (reference), 51st to 70th, 71st to 90th, and 91st to 100th. The primary outcome was a composite of fatal or nonfatal myocardial infarction, or fatal or nonfatal ischemic stroke. Cox proportional hazard modeling was used to assess the association of lipoprotein(a) with the primary outcome. Among 6238 patients with no baseline atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, 45% were women. Women had higher total cholesterol, low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol, and median lipoprotein(a) (33.2 versus 28.9 nmol/L; P<0.001), whereas men had higher rates of diabetes and atrial fibrillation. Higher lipoprotein(a) was associated with an increased incidence of the primary composite outcome, with patients in the 91st to 100th percentile group (≥216 nmol/L) having an adjusted hazard ratio (HR) of 2.07 (95% CI, 1.31–3.25; P<0.01) in women and 2.39 (95% CI, 1.57–3.65; P<0.01) in men, with no interaction based on sex. When examining individual outcomes, the strongest association was present between lipoprotein(a) and fatal or nonfatal myocardial infarction (women: adjusted HR, 2.61 [95% CI, 1.48–4.61]; men: adjusted HR, 3.36 [95% CI, 2.01–5.60]). When stratifying by age, female sex was associated with a lower risk of fatal or nonfatal myocardial infarction in those aged <60 years; however, among older individuals, the risk conferred by elevated lipoprotein(a) was similar between men and women.

Among individuals with no prior atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, elevated lipoprotein(a) is associated with higher rates of cardiovascular outcomes, particularly myocardial infarction, in both women and men.

Keywords: coronary artery disease, lipoprotein(a), myocardial infarction, sex differences

Subject Categories: Primary Prevention, Women

Mass General Brigham

Research Patient Data Registry

## What Is New?

- In patients with no prior atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease within the MGB (Mass General Brigham) Lp(a) Registry, elevated lipoprotein(a) was associated with higher rates of cardiovascular outcomes, particularly myocardial infarction, in both women and men.

- When examining the prognostic value of lipoprotein(a), female sex was associated with a lower risk of fatal or nonfatal myocardial infarction in those aged <60 years; however, among older individuals, the risk between men and women was similar.

## What Are the Clinical Implications?

- Among patients with no history of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, testing for lipoprotein(a) can be used to refine risk of future cardiovascular disease in both women and men.

- Because lipoprotein(a) levels are higher after menopause, women may benefit from repeat lipoprotein(a) testing in older age.

Lipoprotein(a), a low‐density lipoprotein‐like particle in which apolipoprotein B100 is covalently bound to apolipoprotein(a), is a risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), including myocardial infarction (MI) and ischemic stroke. 1 , 2 Genetic association studies and Mendelian randomization analyses have implicated elevated lipoprotein(a) levels as a putative causal risk factor for ASCVD. 3 , 4 Lipoprotein(a) is elevated (≥50 mg/dL or ≥125 nmol/L) in ≈20% of the population, and current US guidelines consider it a risk‐enhancing factor that can be used to guide risk stratification in primary prevention patients. 5 , 6

Prior studies have demonstrated notable sex differences in lipoprotein(a) levels. 7 In an analysis of 36 prospective studies, women had 12% higher lipoprotein(a) concentrations compared with men. 2 However, there is conflicting evidence whether there is a differential relationship between lipoprotein(a) and cardiovascular outcomes in women versus men. One study showed a continuous association of lipoprotein(a) with risk of coronary heart disease that did not vary by sex. 2 Conversely, other analyses suggested that the relation between lipoprotein(a) and ASCVD is more complex in women, with elevated lipoprotein(a) predicting higher cardiovascular risk in only a subset of patients, specifically those with total cholesterol >220 mg/dL. 8

Overall, sex differences in the association of lipoprotein(a) with cardiovascular outcomes have not been well established. Specifically, it remains unclear if an elevation in lipoprotein(a) confers the same increased risk of cardiovascular outcomes in both women and men, particularly for those without prior ASCVD. Historically, women have been treated less aggressively for management of dyslipidemia and coronary artery disease. 9 With clinical trials for targeted lipoprotein(a) therapies currently ongoing, it is a particularly important time to gain further insight into its utility as a biomarker for cardiovascular risk prediction by characterizing the differences in outcomes among women and men with elevated levels of lipoprotein(a). Therefore, in this study, our aim was to evaluate the association of lipoprotein(a) with cardiovascular outcomes among women and men without prior ASCVD.

## METHODS

Because of the sensitive nature of the data collected in this study, requests to access the data set from qualified researchers trained in human subject confidentiality protocols may be sent to the corresponding author.

### Study Population

The design of the MGB (Mass General Brigham) Lp(a) Registry has been previously described. 10 , 11 Briefly, this is a retrospective cohort study from Brigham and Women's Hospital and Massachusetts General Hospital composed of patients aged ≥18 years who had their lipoprotein(a) measured between January 2000 and July 2019 as part of routine clinical care. Exclusion criteria included the following: a diagnosis of severe renal dysfunction, defined as stage 5 chronic kidney disease (CKD) (estimated glomerular filtration rate, <15 mL/min per m2), renal transplant, or on dialysis, or a diagnostic International Classification of Diseases Ninth or Tenth Revision (ICD‐9; ICD‐10) code for a malignant neoplasm during the covariate assessment window, excluding nonmelanoma skin cancers. The MGB Lp(a) Registry was approved by the Institutional Review Board at MGB, and the requirement for informed consent was waived. The present analysis only included patients with no prior ASCVD, defined as history of MI, coronary revascularization, or ischemic stroke, as assessed on the basis of relevant ICD/Current Procedural Terminology codes within the electronic medical record and the use of natural language processing (NLP). Table S1 shows the ICD‐9, ICD‐10, and Current Procedural Terminology codes used to define history of MI, coronary revascularization, and ischemic stroke along with additional details.

### Lipoprotein(a) Assays

The study included patients who underwent lipoprotein(a) testing with the lipoprotein(a) particle assay, measured in nmol/L, or the lipoprotein(a) mass assay, measured in mg/dL. All lipoprotein(a) laboratory testing was performed at certified laboratories over the study period using industry‐standard assays. Because of possible differences in lipoprotein(a) testing techniques over the study period, percentile distributions for each assay were defined separately and then combined across assay types, as done in previous large lipoprotein(a) investigations. 12 Given the well‐established distribution of lipoprotein(a), lipoprotein(a) percentile groups were then generated as 1st to 50th (reference), 51st to 70th, 71st to 90th, and 91st to 100th based on the overall population of patients in the entire MGB Lp(a) Registry. For patients with multiple lipoprotein(a) levels over the study period, the patient was assigned to his/her median lipoprotein(a) level and its corresponding percentile. All analyses were performed using the lipoprotein(a) percentile group as the primary exposure variable. Once assays were combined across percentiles, we subsequently converted all lipoprotein(a) values to nmol/L using the following conversion formula to best represent the data in a clinically relevant manner: lipoprotein(a) nmol = [2.18 × lipoprotein(a)‐M] − 3.83. 13

### Baseline Covariate Assessment

Baseline covariates were determined using data obtained from the MGB RPDR (Research Patient Data Registry), a centralized clinical data registry (comprising demographic data, laboratory data, diagnostic and procedural codes, medical data, vital status, and clinical documentation) that consolidates clinical information from Brigham and Women's Hospital and Massachusetts General Hospital. Vital status was obtained in RPDR from the Social Security Administration Death Master File. For determining cause of death, we used the National Death Index and the Massachusetts Office of Vital Statistics for all patients who were recorded as deceased by the Social Security Administration Death Master File. ICD‐10 codes were characterized to determine the causes of death for each patient who expired during the study follow‐up period. The presence of risk factors was determined by the use of validated NLP algorithms, 14 laboratory data, and diagnostic and procedural ICD‐9, ICD‐10, and Current Procedural Terminology codes. Hypertension was defined by ICD and supplemented by NLP codes. Hyperlipidemia was defined by laboratory‐based definitions using median levels (total cholesterol ≥240 mg/dL, high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol <40 mg/dL [men] and <50 mg/dL [women], low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol ≥160 mg/dL, and triglycerides >175 mg/dL) and supplemented by NLP. Diabetes was defined by hemoglobin A1c, ICD codes, and NLP. The presence of CKD was defined by ICD codes. Smoking status was defined by NLP. Table S1 summarizes the codes used to define the baseline covariates as well as provides further details. Baseline covariates were assessed over the period spanning 12 months before and 30 days after the date of lipoprotein(a) laboratory testing. In individuals with multiple lipoprotein(a) tests, the first chronologic lipoprotein(a) measurement was used to determine the baseline covariate assessment period.

### Sex and Age

Because lipoprotein(a) is known to increase following menopause, 15 , 16 and to better understand the potential impact of changing lipoprotein(a) levels among female patients during menopause, we also analyzed the cohort by dividing all patients into age categories: (1) age ≤50 years, (2) age >50 years but <60 years, and (3) age ≥60 years. We also performed a sensitivity analysis when stratifying our results using age ≥55 versus <55 years, as most women are postmenopausal by this age. 17 Different age categories were used because the exact age of menopause was unable to be ascertained from records in our registry.

### Outcomes

Given several prior studies establishing lipoprotein(a) as a risk factor for MI 18 , 19 and ischemic stroke, 20 , 21 the primary outcome for the analysis was a composite of fatal or nonfatal MI and fatal or nonfatal ischemic stroke. Secondary outcomes included the individual components of the primary outcome, namely, fatal or nonfatal MI, and fatal or nonfatal ischemic stroke. Table S2 summarizes the ICD‐9 and ICD‐10 codes used to define MI and ischemic stroke. Outcomes were ascertained after the baseline covariate period ended (30 days after the date of lipoprotein[a] measurement).

### Statistical Analysis

Continuous variables are reported as mean±SD or median (interquartile range) and compared by sex and lipoprotein(a) percentile groups with Student t‐tests or Mann‐Whitney U tests, as appropriate. Categorical data are reported as counts and percentages and compared across categories of lipoprotein(a) percentile groups with the χ2 test of association or Fisher exact test. Incidence rates were calculated for the primary composite outcome of fatal or nonfatal MI and fatal or nonfatal ischemic stroke, as well as for each of the secondary outcomes. Kaplan‐Meier curves were used to assess the association of lipoprotein(a) percentile categories on primary and secondary outcomes and compared using log‐rank tests. Schoenfeld residuals were used to check for proportional hazards assumptions.

Multivariable Cox proportional hazards modeling was used to assess the association of the lipoprotein(a) percentile categories, with the cardiovascular outcomes mentioned above, and these results were reported as hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% CIs. This modeling was performed for each of the individual subpopulations that were defined by specific sex and age restrictions. In analyses involving individuals from both sexes, both lipoprotein(a) percentile category and biological sex were included as covariates. Spearman rank correlations were used to check for multicollinearity within the multivariable models, which were adjusted for age, race, hypertension, non‐lipoprotein(a) hyperlipidemia, diabetes, CKD status, insulin use (in patients with diabetes), and current or former smoking. We used the Fine‐Gray proportional subhazards model to evaluate the potential for competing risks of noncardiovascular death. Additional analyses also included annual incidence rates of the primary composite outcome and secondary outcome of fatal or nonfatal MI. Furthermore, sensitivity analyses of fatal or nonfatal MI stratified by age, where age groups were defined as ≤50, 51 to 59, and ≥60 years, and also stratified separately by age <55 or ≥55 years, were performed. Age‐related changes in lipoprotein(a) were further evaluated with unadjusted ordinary least squares regression to assess the relationship between the age of the patient at the time of lipoprotein(a) testing and lipoprotein(a) test results. This was done for all patients within the cohort being analyzed and then for men and women separately.

All tests were 2‐tailed and considered statistically significant with P<0.05. All analyses were performed using Stata MP Version 17 (StataCorp, College Station, TX) and RStudio (version 2022.12.0) ggplot2 package (version 3.4.1).

## RESULTS

### Study Population and Baseline Characteristics

The MGB Lp(a) Registry consisted of 16 419 patients, of whom 6238 had no prior ASCVD and were therefore included in this analysis. Among those with no prior ASCVD, 2802 (45%) were women. Baseline characteristics of the population are shown in Table 1. Median age was 55 years in women and 54 years in men (P=0.03). Most (85%) of the total study population self‐identified as non‐Hispanic White. Men had higher rates of diabetes and atrial fibrillation. Rates of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, CKD, and heart failure were similar between the groups. Women had higher median total cholesterol, low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol, and high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol, and lower triglycerides. In addition, women had lower rates of statin use than men (32.6% versus 37.3%; P<0.001).

Median lipoprotein(a) was 33.2 nmol/L in women and 28.9 nmol/L in men (P<0.01). Most participants had lipoprotein(a) within the 1st to 50th percentile (55.6% of women and 60% of men); however, there were more women in the highest percentile group (91st–100th percentile) compared with men (8.6% of all women versus 5.7% of all men; P<0.01). Lipoprotein(a) distribution in men and women is shown in Figure 1A and 1B, respectively, and in Table S3.

### Primary and Secondary Outcomes

Over a median of 12.9 years (interquartile range, 7.7–15.3 years), individuals within the highest lipoprotein(a) percentile group (91st–100th) had a higher incidence of the primary composite outcome of fatal or nonfatal MI, or fatal or nonfatal ischemic stroke in women (HR, 2.63 [95% CI, 1.68–4.12; P<0.01) and men (HR, 2.32 [95% CI, 1.52–3.54]; P<0.01). This association persisted after adjustment for age, race, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, CKD, smoking, and insulin use. Women in the 91st to 100th percentile group (≥216 nmol/L) had an adjusted HR of 2.07 (95% CI, 1.31–3.25; P<0.01) and men in the 91st to 100th percentile group had an adjusted HR of 2.39 (95% CI, 1.57–3.65; P<0.01) for the primary outcome (Table 2), with no interaction by sex (P=0.22; Figure 2A and 2B). The cumulative incidence function of fatal or nonfatal MI or fatal or nonfatal stroke was significantly higher in patients with high lipoprotein(a) than in patients with low lipoprotein(a) after adjusting for other causes of noncardiovascular death as competing risk, as well as adjusting for sex (P<0.001).

When examining the secondary outcome of fatal or nonfatal ischemic stroke, after adjustment, the highest lipoprotein(a) percentile group was associated with an increased incidence in men; incidence of fatal or nonfatal ischemic stroke was also higher in women, although this was not statistically significant. Women in the 91st to 100th percentile group had an HR of 1.79 (95% CI, 0.93–3.44; P=0.08), whereas men in the 91st to 100th percentile had an HR of 2.01 (95% CI, 1.09–3.73; P=0.03) (Table 3), with no interaction based on sex (P=0.27; Figure 3C and 3D).

### Annual Incidence of Outcomes

The annual incidence rate (per 1000 patient‐years) for the primary composite outcome was 17.9 in men in the 91st to 100th percentile group (versus 10.1 in the reference group of 1st–50th percentile) and, similarly, was 17.8 in women in the 91st to 100th percentile group (versus 6.8 in the reference group) (Figure 4A and 4B). Furthermore, the annual incidence rate for fatal or nonfatal MI was 8.5 in men in the 91st to 100th percentile group (versus 2.5 in the reference group) and 5.7 in women (versus 1.7 in the reference group), as shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

*Figure 4: Annual event rates for the primary composite outcome of fatal or nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI) or fatal or nonfatal ischemic stroke (A and B) and secondary outcome of fatal or nonfatal MI (C and D).Annual incidence rates are per 1000 patient‐years.*

### Lipoprotein(a) Stratified by Age

As noted above, for the full cohort, median lipoprotein(a) was significantly higher in women compared with men (33.2 versus 28.9 nmol/L; P<0.01). When evaluating if this phenomenon persists across different age groups, we found that it was not present uniformly (Table S4). Specifically, among individuals at or below the age of 50 years at the time of their first lipoprotein(a) test, women were found to have a higher lipoprotein(a) than their male counterparts (31.0 versus 26.7 nmol/L; P=0.02). Similarly, among individuals aged ≥60 years at the time of their first lipoprotein(a) test, women were also found to have higher lipoprotein(a) than their male counterparts (42.0 versus 28.9 nmol/L; P<0.01). However, among those individuals aged 51 to 59 years, female patients had a numerically lower median lipoprotein(a) compared with their male counterparts (28.9 versus 33.2 nmol/L; P=0.63).

The nature of this age‐related difference was also observed when performing a linear regression evaluating the association of age at initial test date with median lipoprotein(a) value. Although the overall association of age at the time of first lipoprotein(a) testing with median lipoprotein(a) levels was rather modest, there was a significant difference by age. Furthermore, this relationship was only statistically significant among women, for whom every increase in 1 year of age was associated with an increase in the expected median lipoprotein(a) value by 0.14 nmol/L (P<0.01), whereas among men the expected median lipoprotein(a) value only increased by 0.06 nmol/L (P=0.09) (Table S5).

### Outcomes Stratified by Age

To better understand the potential role of menopausal status on the association of lipoprotein(a) with increased cardiovascular risk, we repeated our original multivariable model after dividing the cohort into the following 3 age categories: (1) age ≤50 years, (2) age >50 years but <60 years, and (3) age ≥60 years. With increasing age groups, there was a monotonic increase in the HR of female sex for fatal or nonfatal MI in a model including lipoprotein(a), with women aged ≥60 years no longer having a lower risk when compared with their male counterparts (HR, 0.78 [95% CI, 0.55–1.09]; P=0.15) (Table 4). Similar results were observed when we stratified the population by age <55 years versus age ≥55 years (Table 4).

## DISCUSSION

Our study is one of the largest studies demonstrating the role of lipoprotein(a) as a biomarker for cardiovascular disease risk in both women and men with no prior ASCVD (Figure 5). We evaluated 6238 primary prevention patients, of whom 45% were women, to explore differences in the association of lipoprotein(a) and cardiovascular outcomes based on sex. Our main findings are as follows: (1) elevated lipoprotein(a) is associated with increased cardiovascular outcomes, particularly fatal or nonfatal MI, in both women and men, and (2) the relative risk of fatal or nonfatal MI conferred by having elevated lipoprotein(a) was lower in younger women, but similar between men and women who were aged >60 years. Our results support the biologically plausible hypothesis that female sex may modify the association between elevated lipoprotein(a) and cardiovascular outcomes, thus resulting in younger women being less likely to experience adverse events when compared with younger men.

*Figure 5: Summary of key findings from analysis.aHR indicates adjusted hazard ratio; ASCVD, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; Lp(a), lipoprotein(a); and MI, myocardial infarction.*

Our findings also reinforce that lipoprotein(a) can be used to refine risk of future cardiovascular disease in both women and men. Although prior studies have examined sex differences in the association of lipoprotein(a) with outcomes in large cohorts, such as the Copenhagen General Population study, 22 there have been limited investigations focusing on sex differences solely in the primary prevention patient population. This population is important to examine, as lipoprotein(a) is now increasingly being used as a biomarker to identify higher‐risk patients who do not have known ASCVD. Current ongoing trials are examining the efficacy of lipoprotein(a)‐lowering therapies in secondary prevention populations. If these studies are successful, future trials may focus on primary prevention populations. 23 , 24 Our study shows that both women and men with no prior ASCVD and elevated lipoprotein(a) have similar number of cardiovascular events, which endorses the need to ensure that women are well represented in current and future trials.

In an analysis from the WHS (Women's Health Study), the Women's Health Initiative Observational Study, and the JUPITER (Justification for Use of Statins in Prevention) trial, the clinical utility of lipoprotein(a) was evaluated, which found an association between lipoprotein(a) and outcomes (incident cardiovascular disease: MI, ischemic stroke, coronary revascularization, and cardiovascular death) only among women with total cholesterol >220 mg/dL. 8 The authors concluded that the role of screening for elevated lipoprotein(a) has limited utility in low‐risk women. 8 However, in their analysis, the highest lipoprotein(a) category was >75 mg/dL, which is a lower value than our highest percentile group (~>101 mg/dL). In our study, lipoprotein(a) in the highest percentile group was associated with the composite outcome of fatal or nonfatal MI, or fatal or nonfatal ischemic stroke in both women and men, even after adjustment for covariates such as hyperlipidemia.

When assessing specific cardiovascular outcomes, we demonstrate that higher rates of the composite outcome with elevated lipoprotein(a) were primarily driven by increased rates of fatal or nonfatal MI (adjusted HR of 2.61 in women and 3.36 in men). Conversely, the relationship between elevated lipoprotein(a) and fatal or nonfatal ischemic stroke was less consistent between women and men. The exact pathophysiology to explain these findings is unclear. However, our results are similar to the results observed in an analysis of the Copenhagen General Population Study, in which elevated lipoprotein(a) was associated with an increased risk of MI in both women and men, but there was no association with ischemic stroke. 22 However, this analysis compared lipoprotein(a) subgroups of >40 and <10 mg/dL. 22 Our results demonstrate that even at substantially higher thresholds of lipoprotein(a), the association of lipoprotein(a) and ischemic stroke was weak among patients with no prior ASCVD. Previous studies have also revealed that the association of lipoprotein(a) and ischemic stroke is weaker than the association with other ASCVD outcomes, such as MI. 20 , 24 , 25

As prior reports suggest, lipoprotein(a) levels may be higher in postmenopausal women because of estrogen's ability to suppress transcription of the apolipoprotein(a) gene. 22 , 26 , 27 , 28 We sought to better understand the impact of changing lipoprotein(a) levels among female patients in our cohort by stratifying by age. Categories of women aged ≤50, aged 51 to 59, and aged ≥60 years were used given menopausal status could not be ascertained through electronic records. Notably, our findings show that women aged ≤50 years had higher lipoprotein(a) than men, women aged 51 to 59 had a lipoprotein(a) roughly similar to age‐equivalent men, and women aged ≥60 years had substantially higher lipoprotein(a) than men. The reason behind these differences could not be fully delineated by our analyses, but we postulate that higher lipoprotein(a) in older women is potentially related to the loss of estrogen, and that this result is consistent with other cohorts, such as the Copenhagen General Population study. 22 However, in the Copenhagen cohort, lipoprotein(a) levels were similar in women and men aged 20 to 49 years. 22 The higher lipoprotein(a) values in younger women in our cohort may be related to referral bias, where young women who had lipoprotein(a) tested were, in comparison with young men, more likely to have a higher risk profile, and thus more likely to have elevated lipoprotein(a) levels. Furthermore, we found that lipoprotein(a) level was associated with age at first lipoprotein(a) test in women but not in men, suggesting the role of sex‐specific factors, such as estrogen, in possibly modulating the changes seen in lipoprotein(a) rather than age alone. Given the association of women having higher lipoprotein(a) values in older age, our results and those of others 22 suggest that women may benefit from repeat lipoprotein(a) testing in older age. However, further investigations are warranted to assess these differences in lipoprotein(a) values based on age.

When further evaluating the outcome of fatal or nonfatal MI based on lipoprotein(a) levels, we assessed the hazard of female sex for different age categories. Female sex was associated with a lower risk in those aged <60 years; however, among older individuals, the risk conferred by lipoprotein(a) was similar between men and women. Differences in the hazard of outcomes in younger women, who had either the same (as in those between aged 51 and 59 years) lipoprotein(a) value or only slightly higher (as in those aged ≤50 years) lipoprotein(a) compared with men, may have resulted because of more estrogen as they were more likely to be premenopausal. Hence, our results may be because of a protective effect of estrogen. On the other hand, lipoprotein(a) was significantly higher among women aged ≥60 years and, thus, we hypothesize that the parity of fatal or nonfatal MI rates between men and women in this older age group may be attributable to: (1) a significantly higher lipoprotein(a) among women and (2) the loss of the protective effect of estrogen. Prior work has shown that women taking menopausal hormone therapy have modestly lower levels of lipoprotein(a) than women not taking such treatments, 22 , 29 further supporting the potential relationship between estrogen and lipoprotein(a). However, in a previous analysis, 29 use of hormone therapy did not modify the association of lipoprotein(a) with cardiovascular events, and further work is needed to investigate our hypothesis relating to estrogen's role in driving the age‐related results seen in our study.

There are important limitations of our study to consider, mostly related to the retrospective nature. For one, the population studied was composed of patients from 2 academic hospitals with a predominately White population, and therefore our analyses may not be generalizable to other practice settings and do not reflect racial and ethnic differences in lipoprotein(a). As the study was based in 1 geographic location, our results may not be generalizable to other populations of varying socioeconomic status. Lipoprotein(a) measurement was performed as part of routine care, which may have led to ascertainment bias. In addition, although we adjusted for several baseline covariates, including traditional cardiovascular risk factors, there may still be other unmeasured confounders and, therefore, the sex differences in cardiovascular risk in this analysis cannot be attributed to a single risk factor. Finally, when investigating the differences in lipoprotein(a) levels based on age and presumed menopausal status, we had neither serial data to show changes in lipoprotein(a) within specific individuals nor the exact age of menopause available for women in our cohort.

## CONCLUSIONS

Our study of a large US‐based registry demonstrates that among patients without prior ASCVD, elevated lipoprotein(a) was associated with higher rates of cardiovascular outcomes, particularly MI, in both women and men.
